To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) solving certain pretext tasks (e.g., predicting a missing image pixel) can learn representations that can reduce the sample complexity of a supervised downstream task (e.g., classifying an image) to a provable bound, and (2) the reduction in sample complexity is due to a certain conditional independence assumption on the pretext task that can be verified empirically.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a formal mechanism to explain how solving pretext tasks can help learn representations that are useful for downstream tasks, and provide a theoretical framework to quantify this effect.
we show that solving a self-supervised task can help in learning a representation which can reduce sample complexity of a downstream supervised task.

we prove that solving the pretext task of predicting a missing image channel helps in solving the downstream task of predicting an image class with drastically less samples, if and only if the missing channel is conditionally independent of the image class, conditional on the other channels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
solving pretext tasks with certain conditional independence structure can provably help in solving downstream tasks with drastically lower sample complexity.

the conditional independence between the pretext task and its label is a sufficient condition to learn representations that are useful for solving downstream prediction tasks with drastically reduced sample complexities.

the success of self supervised learning may not just be attributed to the pretext task, but rather to the conditional independence of the pretext task components that enables learning representations that can solve any downstream task.
